cards.title: Pip's Listening Walk
cards.listeningFocus: Environmental sounds and voice sounds — noticing and naming everyday sounds around the garden.
joinIn: The gate: "It did not squeak quietly. It squeaked all the way up, like a question." — make a rising squeak.
The rain: "tapping like tiny feet" — tap fingers lightly on the table.
Moss: "snuffle, snuffle, snuffle" — breathe a snuffling sound through your nose.
Olive: "one long hoot" — a single, held owl hoot.
talkPrompts: What made that sound? Ask before turning the page.
Can you make a snuffling sound like Moss?
Which of the seven sounds was your favourite, and why?

preTeach.note: A short, high, scratchy sound.
A quiet sniffing sound through the nose.

cards.title: Nell's Noisy Hive
cards.listeningFocus: Instrumental sounds and body percussion — making sounds with hands, feet and simple objects.
joinIn: The sticks: "Tap, tap, tap." — tap two fingers together.
The tin: "Boom!" then quietly "Boom." — do both, loud then soft.
The pond slap: "Splat!" — slap a flat hand on your knee.
Stamping and clapping, "faster and faster" — join in and speed up together.
talkPrompts: Which sound was loudest? Which was quietest?
Can you make Boom loud, then Boom quiet, like Nell did?
What is the best sound YOU can make with just your body?

preTeach.note: A group of people making music together.

cards.title: Moss and the Rhyme Pot
cards.listeningFocus: Rhythm and rhyme — hearing when two words chime together.
joinIn: Pause before "frog" (rhymes with "log") and let children supply it.
Pause before "moon" (rhymes with "spoon") and let children supply it.
Pause before "wig" (rhymes with "Fig") and let children supply it.
talkPrompts: If it rhymes with "cat", what could come out of the pot?
Do 'log' and 'frog' sound the same at the end, or the start?
Can you think of your own rhyming pair for the rhyme pot?

preTeach.note: Two words that end with the same sound, like cat and hat.

cards.title: Olive's Sound Game
cards.listeningFocus: Alliteration and oral blending — hearing matching beginnings, and pushing separated sounds back into a word.
joinIn: "S — u — n," said Olive. Children blend: "Sun!"
"N — e — s — t," said Olive. Children blend: "Nest!"
"P — i — p," said Olive. Children blend: "Pip!"
talkPrompts: Pip, pond, pot, petal — what sound do they all start with?
Can you think of another word that starts like Pip?
Try breaking your own name into sounds for a grown-up to blend back together.

preTeach.note: The very first sound in a word.

cards.title: Pip Sat
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 1, week 3 — after s, a, t, p, i, n, m, d (Learning — Phase 2)

preTeach.note: A tap is what water comes out of outside — point to the picture of the brass tap.

prosody.quote: Tap, tap, tap.
prosody.how: Say each "tap" as a short, separate beat, like knocking — a small pause between each one.

questions.q: Where was Pip sitting at the start of the book?
What did Pip do to the puddle?
Why do you think Pip pats the water instead of just sitting still?
What is a tap for?
How do you think Pip is feeling on the last page? How can you tell from the picture?

cards.fluencyNote: With only 4 sounds taught, expect slow, deliberate sound-by-sound reading on every word — that is exactly right at this stage, not a concern.

cards.title: Pip and the Tin
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 1, week 3 — after s, a, t, p, i, n, m, d (Learning — Phase 2)

preTeach.note: A tin here means a small metal container Pip can fit inside — show the picture.

prosody.quote: Pip is in a tin!
prosody.how: Read with surprise — a small lift in pitch on "in" and the exclamation mark.

questions.q: Where does Pip end up sitting?
What does Pip do at the end of the book?
Why might Pip like sitting in the tin?
What does "naps" mean?

cards.fluencyNote: Watch whether Pip's name is read as a whole word or sounded out — by this book it's also fully decodable (p-i-p), so either is fine.

cards.title: Dot the Dog
cards.checkpoint: After s, a, t, p, i, n, m, d, g, o, c, k, ck (Learning — Phase 2, sounds 1-13)

preTeach.note: A mat is a small flat rug — point to the picture if the child is not sure.
A pit here is a small hole Dot has dug, not a stone inside fruit.

prosody.quote: Dot digs. Dot digs a pit.
prosody.how: Match the energy to digging — speed up very slightly on "digs" each time.

questions.q: What is the name of the new dog in this book?
What does Dot dig?
Why do you think Pip and Dot nap at the end?
What is a "pit" in this story?
How do you think Pip feels about getting a new dog?

cards.fluencyNote: Dot's name is fully decodable (d-o-t) — notice whether the child sounds it out confidently rather than guessing from the picture.

cards.title: Fig in the Gap
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds h, b, f, ff

preTeach.note: A gap here is a small space in an old log just big enough for Fig to shelter in.

prosody.quote: Pit, pat. Pit, pat.
prosody.how: Read the pit-pat rhythm like rain — light and even, the same beat each time.

questions.q: Where did Fig find shelter from the rain?
What was Fig doing at the start of the book, before the rain came?
Why do you think Fig felt sad when the rain started?
What is a gap?
How do you think Fig feels by the end of the book, and how can you tell?

cards.fluencyNote: With only 12 sounds taught, expect careful sound-by-sound reading throughout — that is exactly right at this stage.

cards.title: Fig and the Bud
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds h, b, f, ff

preTeach.note: A pip is a small seed — and yes, it is spelled just like Pip the sparrow's name!
A bud is the very first small shoot a seed grows into.

prosody.quote: It got big! Fig got a bud.
prosody.how: Read with a burst of excitement on 'big' — this is the pay-off for all that patient waiting.

questions.q: What did Fig plant in the mud?
What did Fig do while waiting for it to grow?
Why do you think nothing seemed to happen for a while?
What is a bud?
What does this story teach you about waiting for something to grow?

cards.fluencyNote: Watch for confident reading of 'No' — the newest tricky word — as an instantly recognised whole word.

cards.title: Pip Did It
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds h, b, f, ff

preTeach.note: To huff is to breathe out hard, usually from effort.

prosody.quote: Pip huffs. Pip puffs.
prosody.how: Read with real huffing, effortful breaths — lean into the 'h' and 'p' sounds.

questions.q: What was Pip trying to move?
What did Pip do after the first try did not work?
Why do you think Pip kept trying instead of giving up?
What does 'huffs and puffs' mean?
How do you think Pip feels on the very last page, and why?

cards.fluencyNote: Lean into real effort on "huffs" and "puffs" — breathy and strained — with the pace quickening each time Pip tries again.

cards.title: Ned and the Hen
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds h, b, f, ff

preTeach.note: To tug means to pull hard, usually more than once.

prosody.quote: Ned did tug.
prosody.how: Read 'tug' with a short, strong pull in your voice — a single determined effort.

questions.q: What had happened to the hen?
What did Ned do to help?
Why do you think the hen was huffing and puffing?
What does it mean to tug something?
How do you think the hen felt once she was free?

cards.fluencyNote: Give "tug" real physical effort in the voice — a short, strong pull, not a throwaway word — so the rescue actually lands.

cards.title: Fig and the Nut
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds h, b, f, ff

preTeach.note: A nut here is a small hard seed Fig finds on the ground.

prosody.quote: Fig digs and digs.
prosody.how: Say each "digs" with real effort, a little slower the second time, like hard work.

questions.q: What does Fig find on the ground?
Where does the nut end up?
Why does Fig have to dig for the nut?
What does it mean when something is "in mud"?
How do you think Fig feels at the end, napping on the nut?

cards.fluencyNote: Only 16 sounds taught so far — expect careful, sound-by-sound reading on every word, which is exactly right at this stage.

cards.title: Fig and the Fuss
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: Having "a fuss" means getting upset or cross about something small.
Breathing hard and loud, like when you are cross or out of breath.

prosody.quote: Ned huffs and puffs.
prosody.how: Read with real huffing breaths on 'huffs', then a quick puff of air on 'puffs'.

questions.q: Which two characters dig together at the start?
What does Fig tell Ned to do?
Why do you think Ned has a fuss?
How does the story show us Ned feels better by the end?
What does it mean to "have a fuss"?

cards.fluencyNote: First book with four cast names appearing together — check each name is sounded out and blended like any other word (p-i-p, Pip), not guessed or told.

cards.title: Moss Digs
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A den is a small, hidden home an animal digs or makes.

prosody.quote: Dig, dig, dig!
prosody.how: Three short, equally-weighted beats, like real digging — don't rush them into one word.

questions.q: What does Moss dig up?
Who comes to join Moss at the end?
Why do you think Moss and Pip nap after digging?
What is a "den"?

cards.fluencyNote: Only 16 sounds are taught at this point (no h, b, f or l yet) — short, simple sentences are exactly right; do not expect longer reads yet.

cards.title: Nell and the Bell
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: Point to the picture if needed — something that makes a ringing sound when tapped or shaken.

prosody.quote: Nell, Pip and Moss had fun.
prosody.how: Read warmly and a little slower — this is the happy wrap-up line, not an action moment.

questions.q: What colour was Nell's bell?
Where did Pip fall?
How do you think Nell felt when the bell turned out to be fun to share?
The bell makes one sound even though it's spelled with two Ls — what are double letters like this called?

cards.fluencyNote: Watch specifically for ll/ff/ss read as ONE sound, not doubled — the 'll' in 'bell' should sound just like a single 'l'.

cards.title: Fig in the Sun
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A log is a thick piece of wood from a tree.

prosody.quote: Get up, Fig!
prosody.how: A short, encouraging command — a little louder and brighter than the surrounding lines.

questions.q: Where was Fig sitting at the start?
Who comes to find Fig?
Why do you think Fig "had a big fuss"?
What does "had a nap" mean?

cards.fluencyNote: Almost every word here uses single letter-sounds only — a good book to check pure, unrushed sound-by-sound blending with barely any digraphs to distract from it.

cards.title: Nell and the Sap
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: Sap is the sticky liquid that sometimes drips from inside a tree trunk.

prosody.quote: Nip, nip, nip!
prosody.how: Read each "nip" as a short, quick tug — three separate little pulls, not one long sound.

questions.q: What was in the pot under the tree?
What happened to Nell when she sat down?
Why do you think Nell got stuck?
What does "sap" mean?
How did Pip help Nell get free?

cards.fluencyNote: Watch whether 'sap' and 'pot' are blended smoothly rather than read letter by letter in isolation — an early sign of automatic blending.

cards.title: Pip and the Dots
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: Here a dot is a small round seed dropped on the ground, not a mark on paper.

prosody.quote: Pip got a dot. Pip got a dot.
prosody.how: Read the two repeats at an even, steady pace — like Pip hopping from one dot to the next.

questions.q: What was Pip following along the ground?
Who was hiding in the pot?
Why do you think Moss had dropped the dots?
What was Pip following along the ground?
How do you think Pip felt when he found Moss?

cards.fluencyNote: Pip's name is fully decodable by now (p-i-p) — notice whether it is read automatically rather than sounded out each time.

cards.title: Ned Digs a Gift
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: Here a cap means a small bottle cap found buried in the gravel, not a hat.

prosody.quote: Ned got a cap!
prosody.how: Read with a burst of surprise and delight on 'cap' — this is Ned's big find.

questions.q: What did Ned find while digging?
What did Ned do with the cap?
Why do you think Ned wanted to give the cap to Nell?
What does it mean to tap something?
How do you think Nell felt about her gift?

cards.fluencyNote: Contrast the quiet, steady pace of the digging pages with the sudden burst of excitement on "Ned got a cap!" — that change in pace is what makes the find land.

cards.title: The Sun on the Wall
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A flat rock like this really does warm up in the sun — that is why so many small creatures like to sit on one.

prosody.quote: Moss, Fig and Pip sat in the sun.
prosody.how: Read the list of three names with a little rise on each one, then settle on 'sat in the sun'.

questions.q: Who got onto the rock first?
How many friends ended up sharing the rock?
Why do you think the rock was a popular spot?
What does it mean for something to get warm in the sun?
Why might three friends want to share one small rock instead of finding three different ones?

cards.fluencyNote: Read the three names with a small rise on each, as if they're arriving one after another, then let the pace settle and relax on "sat in the sun" — the voice should visibly unwind.

cards.title: Nell Hums
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A hum is the quiet buzzing sound some small bugs make.

prosody.quote: Hums, hums, hums!
prosody.how: Read each 'hums' smooth and steady, almost like humming it yourself.

questions.q: What was Nell trying to find?
What did Nell do instead of running around looking?
Why did sitting still and listening help Nell more than searching?
What does it mean to hum?
What is this story teaching you about using your ears, not just your eyes?

cards.fluencyNote: The repeated "Hums, hums, hums" should sound smooth and sustained, almost like an actual hum, rather than three separate clipped words.

cards.title: Fig Tidies Up
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A mess means things are left scattered about, not tidy.

prosody.quote: It is a mess!
prosody.how: Read with a surprised, slightly dismayed tone — Fig has just spotted the problem.

questions.q: What two things does Fig find in the mess?
Where does Fig put the pot and the cup?
Why do you think the pots and cups were left on the log?
What does "tidies" mean?
How do you think Fig feels on the last page, and why?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 5-6 repeat the same sentence shape with just one word changed ("pot"/"cup") — a good spot to notice how quickly the second line gets easier to read.

cards.title: Nell and the Log
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds l, ll, ss

preTeach.note: A den here is the small space inside the log where Nell rests.

prosody.quote: Nell can hum a lot.
prosody.how: Hum gently through the word "hum" itself, like a real buzzing bee.

questions.q: What kind of bug is Nell?
Where does Nell have her den?
Why might a gap in a log make a good den for a bee?
What is a "den"?
Why do you think lots of different bugs nap in the same log?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book with short, fact-like sentences — encourage a clear, matter-of-fact reading tone rather than a storytelling one.

cards.title: Olive and the Sun Pot
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: Here the gap is a shady space between shelves where no sunlight reaches.

prosody.quote: The pot is not sad!
prosody.how: Read with real relief and delight — this is the moment Olive's mistake is fixed.

questions.q: Where did Moss put his pot?
Where did Olive put her pot at first?
Why do you think the plant in the gap was not happy?
What is the tricky word in this book that cannot be sounded out?
What did Olive learn from copying Moss?

cards.fluencyNote: This is the first book with 'the' — check it is read instantly as a whole word, not sounded out letter by letter.

cards.title: Olive in the Gap
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 2: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: A fuss here means a noisy commotion.

prosody.quote: A pot fell! A cap fell!
prosody.how: Read each exclamation with a sudden, sharp drop in pitch, like something toppling.

questions.q: What two things fell over when the wind picked up?
Where did Olive shelter?
Why do you think Olive chose to stay in the gap rather than go somewhere else?
What is the newest tricky word in this book?
How can you tell from the story that the weather is calming down?

cards.fluencyNote: Match the voice to the weather: sharp and sudden on "A pot fell! A cap fell!", then let the pace and pitch settle as the wind dies down by the end.

cards.title: Moss and the Web
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: The van here is a small toy van left out in the garden grass.

prosody.quote: No! Moss will not rip the web.
prosody.how: Read 'No!' firmly, then slow down on 'will not rip the web' — Moss is being careful.

questions.q: Where was the web?
What did Moss sit on while he waited?
Why did Moss decide not to climb on the van?
The web was wet at the start. What made it dry?
Why was it a good thing that the web was still there at the end?

cards.fluencyNote: The first j/v/w words appear here — notice whether 'jug', 'van' and 'web' are blended smoothly as these new sounds join the mix.

cards.title: Fig Gets Up
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: If a web rips, the thin thread breaks.

prosody.quote: The web did rip. Fig fell!
prosody.how: Read with a sudden dip in your voice on 'fell', as if tumbling down with Fig.

questions.q: What did Fig try to climb on at the start?
What happened the first time Fig tried to climb up?
Why do you think Fig tried again instead of staying on the ground?
What does it mean when a web 'rips'?
How is this story similar to Pip Did It?

cards.fluencyNote: Let the voice visibly dip on "Fig fell!", then pick back up with renewed energy on the second climb — the two attempts should sound different.

cards.title: Nell and the Jug
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: To sip means to drink a very small amount at a time.

prosody.quote: Nell did sip a lot.
prosody.how: Read 'a lot' with a satisfied little stretch, as if Nell really is enjoying her drink.

questions.q: What was Nell drinking from?
Why do you think the jug was wet?
Why might a bee need to drink water on a hot day?
What does 'sip' mean?
What real fact about bees does this story teach you?

cards.fluencyNote: Stretch "a lot" out with real satisfaction, like Nell genuinely enjoying a long drink — contrast it with the shorter, plainer lines around it.

cards.title: Pip and the Jog
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: To jog means to run at a steady, gentle pace — exactly what Pip and Ned are doing in their race.

prosody.quote: Ned got wet in mud!
prosody.how: Read with a sudden, splashy surprise on 'wet in mud' — the race takes an unexpected turn here.

questions.q: What happened to Ned during the race?
Who reached the end of the path first?
Why do you think Pip went back to sit with Ned instead of staying at the finish?
What does it mean to jog?
What is the same about this story and Nell's Race?

cards.fluencyNote: Give "Ned got wet in mud!" a sudden, surprised jolt in pace and pitch — the race's rhythm should audibly break there, then settle again once Pip goes back for Ned.

cards.title: All About Moss
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: A den here is a cosy hiding place Moss makes out of leaves to sleep in.

prosody.quote: Moss has a lot of pins.
prosody.how: Read "a lot" with emphasis — this is the book's first fact, so give it weight.

questions.q: What covers Moss's back?
What does Moss dig up to eat?
Why might Moss need to nap a lot if he digs for food?
What is a den?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: This is a non-fiction book — read each page as a stated fact, with a small pause before moving to the next one, rather than as a flowing story.

cards.title: Pip and the Jam
cards.checkpoint: Reception Autumn 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds j, v, w

preTeach.note: A bird's bill is its beak — Pip gets jam stuck right on his.

prosody.quote: Pip has jam on his bill!
prosody.how: Read with a surprised little gasp on "jam on his bill" — this is the funny turn in the story.

questions.q: What does Pip find in the pot?
How does Pip get the jam off his bill?
Why do you think Pip goes straight back to the jam at the end?
What is a bill?
Does Pip mind getting jam on his bill? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: Page 5 is the surprise peak of the story — give it the most energy, then settle the pace again for the calmer clean-up on pages 6-7.

cards.title: Ned's Box of Bits
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds x, y, z

preTeach.note: Fit means something is the right size to go into a space — Ned's rock does not fit at first.

prosody.quote: Ned gets a big rock. It will not fit!
prosody.how: Read with surprise and a rising pitch on "not fit" — a small problem appearing.

questions.q: What three things does Ned put in his box?
What does Ned do when the rock will not fit?
Why did digging a bigger hole help the rock go in?
What does "fit" mean?
How can you tell Ned does not give up easily?

cards.fluencyNote: The repeated "Ned gets a ___. Ned pops it in." pattern across pages 3-4 is a good one to read with matching rhythm both times.

cards.title: Olive and Fig in the Barn
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds x, y, z

preTeach.note: A sack is a big soft bag made of cloth, like the one Fig ends up sitting in.

prosody.quote: Fig! Fig!
prosody.how: Read as a real call across a big space — loud, with a gap between the two calls.

questions.q: Where did Olive and Fig go at the start?
Where was Fig hiding in the end?
Why did Olive check on top of things and inside the pot first?
What is a sack?
How do you think Olive felt when she found Fig?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 3-5 are a little search sequence — slow the pace slightly here to build a touch of suspense before the reveal on page 6.

cards.title: Pip Finds Nell
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds x, y, z

preTeach.note: A window box is a long container of plants that sits on a windowsill.

prosody.quote: Nell is in the pot!
prosody.how: Read with surprise — a little lift in pitch and energy on this page, since it is the twist in the story.

questions.q: What is Pip hopping along?
What does Pip find at the very end of the box?
Why do you think Pip keeps hopping on after each bit?
What does it mean to "pick something up"?
How do you think Pip feels when he sees Nell in the pot?

cards.fluencyNote: The repeated pattern "Pip hops on. Pip gets a bit." on two pages is a good spot to practise matching pace across a repeated sentence shape.

cards.title: Ned and the Bag
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds x, y, z

preTeach.note: Gravel is lots of small stones, like the ones on the path Ned hops along.

prosody.quote: Nell hums. Nell has fun.
prosody.how: Read both short sentences warmly and a little slower, landing softly on "fun" to close the story.

questions.q: How many bits does Ned find in total?
Who does Ned give the bag to?
Why do you think Ned wanted to collect bits in the first place?
What is a "bag" for?
How do you know Nell is pleased with the bag?

cards.fluencyNote: Ned's counting page ("Ned gets six bits") is a good spot to point at each word while reading, matching one spoken word to one printed word.

cards.title: Pip and Fig at the Pond
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds x, y, z

preTeach.note: Being "in a fix" means being stuck and unable to get free.

prosody.quote: Fig pops up!
prosody.how: Read with a sudden burst of relief and delight, after the slower, effortful tugging lines before it.

questions.q: Where does Fig get stuck?
Who helps Fig get free?
Why do you think Pip keeps tugging even when it does not work at first?
What does it mean to be "in a fix"?
How do you think Fig feels on the last page?

cards.fluencyNote: With only 32 sounds taught, expect careful sound-by-sound reading throughout — that is exactly right at this stage.

cards.title: Nell and the Wig
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds zz, qu, ch

preTeach.note: A wig is fake hair you can wear — point to the picture.
A quiz is a set of questions to answer, often as a game.

prosody.quote: Zip, zap! Nell can zip up.
prosody.how: Make "Zip, zap!" quick and snappy, like the sound of a zip.

questions.q: What colour was Nell's wig?
What did Nell do well?
Why might Nell want to wear a wig?
What sound do the two letters "qu" make together?

cards.fluencyNote: New sounds here are all consonants (j, v, w, x, y, z, zz, qu) — listen especially for 'x' as /ks/ at the end of 'six', easy to mis-read as a single sound.

cards.title: Nell Waits Out the Wet
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds zz, qu, ch

preTeach.note: Zips here means moves very fast, the way a zip fastener closes in one quick movement.

prosody.quote: Nell is quick. Nell zips into a box.
prosody.how: Pick up the pace on "zips into a box" to match how fast Nell moves.

questions.q: Why does Nell go into the box?
Who does Nell share the box with?
Why does Nell come out again at the end?
What does "zips" mean in this story?
How can you tell the weather has changed between page 2 and page 7?

cards.fluencyNote: The "Nell can buzz" pattern opens and closes the book — read both the same cheerful way so the ending echoes the start.

cards.title: All About Ned
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds zz, qu, ch

preTeach.note: Quack is the sound a duck makes — it is also the word for making that sound.

prosody.quote: Ned has fun. Ned quacks!
prosody.how: Read "Ned quacks!" loudly with a real quacking energy to finish.

questions.q: What sound can Ned make?
What does Ned dig for in the mud?
Why does a duckling need a big bill?
What does "quacks" mean?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book again — read each short fact clearly and separately, pausing between pages rather than running them together.

cards.title: Olive's Gift for Fig
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds sh, th, ng

preTeach.note: A shell is the hard, curved case left behind by a small sea or garden creature.

prosody.quote: Olive hops to Fig.
prosody.how: Read with a light, pleased little bounce — Olive is pleased with her gift.

questions.q: What two things does Olive put in the bag?
Who is the gift for?
Why do you think Olive chose a shell and a ring rather than something else?
What is a shell?
How do you think Fig feels when he looks in the bag?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 3-4 name one new object each — read them at an even pace so each gift gets its own moment before the bag is sealed on page 5.

cards.title: The Long Path
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds sh, th, ng

preTeach.note: A dash is a short, quick run.

prosody.quote: Moss and Pip dash on the path.
prosody.how: Speed up slightly on "dash" to match the quick movement, then slow again for the calm ending.

questions.q: What is wrong with Moss's path at first?
Who helps Moss finish the path?
Why was Moss's path a mess when he dug it alone?
What does "dash" mean?
What does this story show about working together?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 1-3 contrast Pip's neat path with Moss's messy one — read page 3 a little more hesitantly to match the wobblier result.

cards.title: Olive and the Pot
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds sh, th, ng

preTeach.note: A shed here is a small wooden hut where plant pots are kept.

prosody.quote: Olive is sad.
prosody.how: Read slowly and quietly, with a dip in tone, to match how Olive feels after the mix-up.

questions.q: What is Moss doing at the start of the book?
Whose pot does Olive dig in by mistake?
Why does Olive feel sad after digging in that pot?
What does it mean when something "is a mess"?
How does Olive solve the problem by the end of the book?

cards.fluencyNote: First book with "sh" — listen for it read as one single sound in "shed", not spelled out as two separate letters.

cards.title: Ned and the Fish
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ai, ee, igh

preTeach.note: A dash is a sudden, quick run.
Moving in sharp side-to-side turns, like a lightning-bolt shape.

prosody.quote: A fish! The fish was red.
prosody.how: Read "A fish!" as a sudden, excited burst, then slow right down and calm for the second sentence.

questions.q: What colour was the fish Ned caught?
What did Ned and his pals do with the fish at the end?
Why did Ned decide to put the fish back?
What does "zigzag" mean? Can you show me with your finger?
How do you think the fish felt when it got back in the water?

cards.fluencyNote: First appearance of ch/sh/th/ng — listen for these said as ONE sound, not spelled out letter by letter (e.g. 'sh', not 's-h').

cards.title: All About Nell
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ai, ee, igh

preTeach.note: Buzz is the low humming sound a bee makes with its wings.

prosody.quote: Nell is wet in the rain.
prosody.how: Read with a slightly flat, unhappy tone — this is the one page where things are not going well for Nell.

questions.q: What sound can Nell make?
What happens to Nell when it rains?
Why does Nell wait instead of flying in the rain?
What does "buzz" mean?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: Notice the shift in mood from sunny (pages 4-5) to wet (pages 6-7) and back to sunny again — let your voice follow that change.

cards.title: Pip and the Tapping Tub
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ai, ee, igh

preTeach.note: To peek means to take a quick, careful look at something.

prosody.quote: Is it Ned? Is it Nell?
prosody.how: Read both questions with real curiosity, a little rising at the end of each.

questions.q: What sound does Pip hear?
Who is making the tapping sound?
Why does Pip choose not to peek at first?
What does "peek" mean?
What does Pip work out just by listening, before he looks?

cards.fluencyNote: The "Tap, tap, tap" line and the two guessing questions are a good place to practise pausing for real curiosity, not rushing to the answer.

cards.title: Ned Pegs the Rail
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ai, ee, igh

preTeach.note: Pegs are the small clips used to fix washing onto a rail so it does not blow away.

prosody.quote: Ned did it! Ned did a big job.
prosody.how: Read with pride and a strong beat on "big job" — Ned has finished something he is proud of.

questions.q: What does Ned peg onto the rail?
How many bits does Ned peg up in total?
Why might Ned feel proud of a job that sounds so small?
What are pegs for?
What does Ned do once the job is finished?

cards.fluencyNote: The counting-up feel of pages 3-5 works well read a little slower, one peg at a time, before the pace relaxes for the nap on page 8.

cards.title: Olive and the Lost Pin
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 1, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ai, ee, igh

preTeach.note: To quit means to stop trying before you are finished.

prosody.quote: Olive did not quit.
prosody.how: Read slowly and firmly — this is the determined turning point of the story.

questions.q: What does Olive lose on the path?
What does Olive do to try to find it?
Why does Olive go back along the same path instead of a new one?
What does "quit" mean?
What does this story show about not giving up?

cards.fluencyNote: The two questions on page 5 ("Is the pin on this bit?... that bit?") suit a searching, hopeful tone each time, even though the answer keeps being no.

cards.title: Rain on the Oak
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds oa, oo, oo (book)

preTeach.note: A kind of large tree.

prosody.quote: I can see his feet!
prosody.how: Read with delight — a rising, excited tone, leaning on "feet".

questions.q: What animal sat up high in the oak tree?
Where did Pip see Ned at the end?
Why was the goat's coat wet?
What does "high" mean? Can you point to something high up in the room?
What do you think the weather was like in this story? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: Four new long-vowel teams land in one book (ai, ee, igh, oa) — expect reading to slow right down on words with those teams even if everything else is fast; that is the new content, not a regression.

cards.title: Moss and the Cool Days
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds oa, oo, oo (book)

preTeach.note: Soon means something will happen before very long, but not right now.

prosody.quote: Soon it will not be hot.
prosody.how: Read "soon" with a slight forward lean in your voice, as if looking ahead.

questions.q: What does Moss dig for in the mud?
What does Moss do more of as it gets cooler?
Why might Moss need more naps when there is less food about?
What does "soon" mean?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book — pages 6-7 both start with "Soon", so read them as two separate, calmly stated facts rather than rushing one into the other.

cards.title: Fig and the Pod
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds oa, oo, oo (book)

preTeach.note: A pod is the curled, dried case that falls from some plants and trees.

prosody.quote: The pod can bob on the pool.
prosody.how: Read "bob" with a light up-and-down bounce in your voice.

questions.q: Why does Fig want to get across the pool?
What does Fig use instead of a boat?
Why does Fig choose a pod rather than waiting for a real boat?
What is a pod?
How can you tell Fig's plan worked?

cards.fluencyNote: Page 6 is the calm middle of the crossing — read it steadily and gently, then lift your voice for the arrival on page 7.

cards.title: Moss and the Cool Pool
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 1 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds oa, oo, oo (book)

preTeach.note: A pool here is a small puddle of water collected on top of a wall.

prosody.quote: Moss, the fox and the goat sip.
prosody.how: Read slowly, giving each name its own little pause, so all three animals are clearly heard sharing the water.

questions.q: Why is Moss hot at the start?
Name two other animals who visit the pool.
Why might lots of different animals want to drink from the same pool on a hot day?
What does "cool" mean?
Is this story make-believe or a true fact book? How can you tell?

cards.fluencyNote: First book with long and short "oo" together (pool/good) — listen for the child noticing these sound slightly different even though spelled the same way.

cards.title: The Dark Farm
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ar, or, ur

preTeach.note: A place where animals and crops are kept and grown.

prosody.quote: It was dark on the farm.
prosody.how: Read slowly and quietly to set a night-time mood — almost a whisper.

questions.q: What did the fox run to?
What did Ned take off before getting in the pool?
Why do you think it was hard to see on the farm?
The story says the moon is "far, far up" — what does "far" mean?
Why might the fox have wanted the corn?

cards.fluencyNote: 'oo' appears with two different sounds in this half-term's set (moon vs good) — notice whether each instance gets the right one for that word, rather than one generic guess.

cards.title: The Big Farm
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ar, or, ur

preTeach.note: A farm building for animals or storing hay.

prosody.quote: Go to the barn, Ned!
prosody.how: A firm, urging instruction — lean on "Go" and "barn".

questions.q: What two animals does Ned wonder about?
Who did Ned find in the corn?
Why do you think it got dark while Ned was out?
What does "ran far" mean?

cards.fluencyNote: ar/or/ur all appear — check they aren't collapsed into one generic 'er' sound; each should sound distinctly different.

cards.title: Nell's Fork in the Oak
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ar, or, ur

preTeach.note: A fork in a tree is the spot where a branch splits into two, like Nell's landing spot.

prosody.quote: Nell did sit on the fork!
prosody.how: Read with a triumphant little lift on "sit on the fork" — the second try has worked.

questions.q: What does Nell try to land on?
What happens the first time Nell buzzes up?
Why does Nell turn back down instead of landing anyway?
What is a fork in a tree?
What does Nell do differently that makes the second try work?

cards.fluencyNote: The two "Nell buzzes up" lines on pages 3 and 6 are identical — read the first with uncertainty and the second with more confidence, since the reader already knows how it ends.

cards.title: Pip and the Curly Shell
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 2 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ar, or, ur

preTeach.note: A curl is a tight, round, spiral shape, like the one on the shell Pip finds.

prosody.quote: It is a shell!
prosody.how: Read with a satisfied little exclamation — the mystery is finally solved.

questions.q: What does Pip find on the branch?
What two things does Pip wonder if it might be?
Why does Pip turn the object over and look closely instead of guessing straight away?
What does "curl" mean?
What clue tells Pip it is not a nut?

cards.fluencyNote: Page 6's two questions suit a genuinely puzzled tone — slow down slightly there before the confident answer on page 7.

cards.title: Rain and the Moon
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: The sound an owl makes, more than once.

prosody.quote: Look! The moon is high.
prosody.how: A sudden, delighted "Look!", then slow down to really stretch the "oo" in "moon".

questions.q: Where did Nell and Olive keep dry?
What happens to the moon by the end of the story?
Why do you think the rain made Nell and Olive want to stay in the oak?
What does "soon" mean?

cards.fluencyNote: Five long-vowel teams in one book (ai, ee, igh, oa, oo) — good for checking each gets its OWN sound, not a single generic 'long vowel' guess.

cards.title: Olive's Rainy-Day Box
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: A coin is a small, round piece of money.

prosody.quote: Rain is near.
prosody.how: Read with a slightly lower, watchful tone — a hint of what is coming.

questions.q: What three things does Olive collect?
Where does Olive put the box to keep it dry?
Why does Olive collect the box of bits before the rain comes, not after?
What is a coin?
How do you think Olive feels, sitting under the hedge with her full box?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 3-5 each introduce one found object at the same steady pace — save the quicker, more urgent tone for "Rain is near" on page 6.

cards.title: Moss Calls for Nell
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: To hum means to make a long, low sound with your voice, without saying words.

prosody.quote: Moss can hear Nell hum!
prosody.how: Read with a relieved, happy lift — Moss has finally found a clue to where Nell is.

questions.q: Where are Moss and Nell at the start of the story?
How does Moss find Nell again?
Why does Moss check both the pool and the oak while he looks?
What does "hums" mean?
Why might listening help Moss find Nell when looking has not?

cards.fluencyNote: The two questions on page 5 work well read with real searching energy, slowing slightly before the hopeful discovery on page 7.

cards.title: Fig and the Big Pot
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: A cart is a simple wooden vehicle on wheels, used for carrying heavy things like the big pot.

prosody.quote: Ned and Fig tip the pot. The pot turns!
prosody.how: Build the effort into your voice across both sentences, then land firmly on "turns!" for the success.

questions.q: What is Fig trying to move?
Who comes to help Fig?
Why could Fig not tip the pot alone?
What is a cart?
What does this story show about asking for help?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 3-4 repeat "Fig can not tip it" — read both with real effort and strain, so the success on page 7 feels earned.

cards.title: Fig and the Seed
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: A shoot is the first thin green stem that grows up out of a seed.

prosody.quote: Fig waits. A shoot pops up.
prosody.how: Pause clearly after "waits" to show time passing, then read "pops up" brightly and quickly.

questions.q: Where does Fig first see the seed?
What comes up out of the soil first — the root or the shoot?
Why does Fig have to wait so many times in this book?
What is a "bud"?
Is this story telling you something true about how plants grow?

cards.fluencyNote: The repeated "Fig waits." across several pages is a good spot to practise a slow, patient reading pace rather than rushing through a repeated line.

cards.title: Ned and the Rain
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 3 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds ow, oi, ear

preTeach.note: A den is a small, hidden shelter — here, a cosy spot at the base of the oak.

prosody.quote: Ned can hear the rain.
prosody.how: Read quietly, almost a whisper, then let the pace quicken on the next line as Ned hurries down.

questions.q: Where is Ned sitting at the start of the book?
Where does Ned go when he hears the rain?
How does Ned know the rain is coming before it starts?
What does it mean when the book says Ned "runs down"?
How do you know Ned's den kept him dry?

cards.fluencyNote: Phase 3 is now complete — a smooth read of ear/air/ure/er words here is good evidence the whole phase is secure.

cards.title: The Owl and the Cow
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds air, ure, er

preTeach.note: A farm building where animals or hay are kept.

prosody.quote: Now it is dark and cool.
prosody.how: Slow, settled pace — this is a calm, scene-setting line, not an exciting one.

questions.q: Which two animals does Pip see in this book?
What did Pip find in the soil?
Why do you think Pip and Olive look down at the cow together at the end?
What is a "pair" of horns? How many is a pair?
How does the story show it's night-time?

cards.fluencyNote: A smooth read here is real evidence the Phase 3 digraphs are secure, not just the newest sounds.

cards.title: Down at the Pool
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds air, ure, er

preTeach.note: Soil is the earth or ground plants grow in.

prosody.quote: See you soon!
prosody.how: A warm, friendly goodbye — let the voice lift slightly on "soon".

questions.q: What did Ned find in the soil?
Who sat on a chair in this story?
Why do you think Ned "turns to go" near the end?
What does "near dark" mean about the time of day?

cards.fluencyNote: This book completes Phase 3 — if the last six teams (ow, oi, ear, air, ure, er) all read smoothly, that is real evidence the whole phase is secure.

cards.title: Fun at the Fair
cards.checkpoint: Reception Spring 2, week 4 — Learning — Phase 3: new sounds air, ure, er

preTeach.note: A fair is a fun outdoor event with rides, games and stalls.
"Corn on the cob" means corn still on its stick-shaped core.

prosody.quote: The fair was good fun.
prosody.how: A satisfied, happy close — slow and warm, not rushed.

questions.q: What did Nell have to eat at the fair?
What colour hat did Fig get?
Why do you think the chair at the fair was "up high"?
What is a "cheer"?

cards.fluencyNote: A genuinely mixed Phase 3 review book — good for checking whether any one team still slows reading down, before moving on to Phase 4.

cards.title: Fig Shares the Bun
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 1 — Phase 4: CVCC words: two consonant sounds together at the end (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: Munch means to chew something noisily and happily.

prosody.quote: Fig, Ned and Nell munch the bun.
prosody.how: Read "munch" with a satisfied, chewy sound in your voice.

questions.q: Who does Fig share the bun with?
How many friends get a bit of the bun?
Why do Ned and Nell look at the bun on page 3?
What does "munch" mean?
How do you think Fig feels about sharing by the end?

cards.fluencyNote: Pages 5-6 repeat the same sentence shape for Ned and then Nell — read them at matching pace and warmth to show the sharing is fair.

cards.title: All About Growing
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 1 — Phase 4: CVCC words: two consonant sounds together at the end (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: Soil is the dark earth that plants grow in.

prosody.quote: A shoot pops up.
prosody.how: Read "pops up" with a small, sudden lift — this is the moment the plant first appears.

questions.q: What does Ned put into the soil?
What two things does the seed need to grow?
Why does the root grow down while the shoot grows up?
What is soil?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book that follows one seed from page 2 to page 8 — read it as a single unfolding sequence of facts, in order, rather than separate unrelated statements.

cards.title: Pip and Ned at the Gap
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 1 — Phase 4: CVCC words: two consonant sounds together at the end (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A gap here is the space in a fence or hedge that the two friends run to.

prosody.quote: Pip and Ned have fun.
prosody.how: Read warmly and a little playfully, to show the race ends happily for both of them, not just the winner.

questions.q: Who gets to the gap first?
What does Pip do once he gets there?
Why does Pip wait for Ned instead of going off without him?
What does it mean to "wait for" someone?
What does this story suggest matters more than winning a race?

cards.fluencyNote: The parallel lines "Pip hops fast."/"Ned hops fast too." are a good spot to practise matching rhythm and pace across two similar sentences.

cards.title: Ned in the Frost
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A trek is a long walk or journey.
A ramp is a slope you can walk or climb up, rather than steps.

prosody.quote: Splash! Ned fell in with a plop.
prosody.how: Say "Splash!" sharply and suddenly, then let "plop" land softer and rounder.

questions.q: What happened to Ned when he tried to jump the pond?
Who helped Ned up the ramp?
Why was the grass described as "crisp" and "stiff"?
What does "damp" mean?
How do you think Ned felt after falling in, since the book says he "was glad"?

cards.fluencyNote: No new sounds here — the whole point is blending longer words with two consonants together (f-r-o-s-t, c-r-i-s-p). Listen for each consonant sounded separately, not squashed into one guess.

cards.title: Fun in the Wind
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A gust is a sudden, strong rush of wind.
To cling means to hold on tightly.

prosody.quote: The wind did stop at last.
prosody.how: Let the pace slow and settle on this final line, after faster, excited lines before it.

questions.q: What did Pip have to do in the wind?
Where did Pip and Nell run to shelter?
Why do you think it was "snug in the shed"?
What does "gust" mean?

cards.fluencyNote: Phase 4: no new sounds. Listen for every consonant said as its own sound, then blended into the whole word — none dropped, none squashed into its neighbour.

cards.title: Nell Flies to the Bloom
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A bloom is another word for a flower, especially one that is fully open.

prosody.quote: Nell can buzz to a bright bloom.
prosody.how: Read "bright bloom" with a touch of delight — this is a happy discovery.

questions.q: What can you see on Nell's body?
What does Nell collect from the bloom?
Why does Nell bring the stuff back to her pals instead of keeping it herself?
What is a bloom?
Is this book make-believe or true? How do you know?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book with a clear journey — out to the bloom, then back to the pals — read pages 2-5 and pages 6-7 as two matching halves of one trip.

cards.title: Pip and the Frog in the Rain
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A gap is a small space or opening, just big enough to shelter in out of the rain.

prosody.quote: Drip, drip, drip.
prosody.how: Read each "drip" as a separate, even beat, like the sound of real rainfall, both times it appears.

questions.q: Where does Pip shelter from the rain?
Who else is already sheltering in the gap?
Why do Pip and the frog wait together instead of each going off alone?
What is a gap?
How can you tell the rain has eased by the end of the story?

cards.fluencyNote: The repeated "Drip, drip, drip" on pages 2 and 5 is a good spot to practise matching rhythm and pace on a repeated line.

cards.title: Nell and the Sock
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: A rail here is a washing line — a rail where wet clothes are hung up to dry.

prosody.quote: Nell and Fig clap and clap.
prosody.how: Read with a bright, bouncy rhythm on the repeated "clap and clap" to match the celebration.

questions.q: What is blocking Nell’s view on the rail?
How does Nell find Fig if she cannot see him?
Why does listening help Nell when looking does not?
What does "past" mean in "gets past the sock"?
How do you think Nell and Fig feel when they finally meet?

cards.fluencyNote: Phase 4: no new sounds. Listen for every consonant in "clap" said as its own sound, then blended into the whole word — none dropped, none squashed into its neighbour.

cards.title: Fig and the Black Box
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: Bricks are small hard blocks used for building — Fig finds a box full of them.

prosody.quote: Fig claps and claps.
prosody.how: Read with real delight and a steady, happy rhythm to close the book on a proud note.

questions.q: What is inside the black box?
How many bricks does Fig bring to the top?
Why does Fig carry the bricks one at a time instead of all together?
What does "brings" mean?
How can you tell Fig feels proud by the end?

cards.fluencyNote: A longer-word practice book — "bricks" and "brings" both blend four sounds in a row; slow, clear blending matters more here than speed.

cards.title: Pip and the Gap
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: To prop something up means to lean it against or under something else to hold it steady.

prosody.quote: Pip claps. Pip did it!
prosody.how: Read with a sudden burst of pride and energy, landing hard on "did it".

questions.q: What is wrong with the gap at the start?
What does Pip use to fix the gap?
Why does Pip have to hop off and look for something first?
What does "flat" mean?
How do you know Pip is pleased with the fix at the end?

cards.fluencyNote: Phase 4: no new sounds. Listen for every consonant in "flat" said as its own sound, then blended into the whole word — none dropped, none squashed into its neighbour.

cards.title: Ned Helps a Bug
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: When mud "grips" something, it holds on tight and will not let go easily.

prosody.quote: Ned digs and digs.
prosody.how: Read with steady, effortful energy, a touch slower the second time, like real digging.

questions.q: Where is the bug stuck at the start?
What does Ned do to free the bug?
Why can the bug not get up by itself?
What does "soft" mean when talking about mud?
What is the true fact this book is teaching about mud?

cards.fluencyNote: A non-fiction book ending on a fact rather than a feeling — encourage a clear, confident tone on the final sentence rather than rushing past it.

cards.title: Olive and the Wind
cards.checkpoint: Reception Summer 1, week 2 — Phase 4: CCVC words: two consonant sounds together at the start (no new sounds)

preTeach.note: This describes a strong wind blowing hard and loud, almost like heavy breathing.

prosody.quote: The wind huffs and puffs.
prosody.how: Read with real huffing and puffing breaths, loud and a little blustery, then calm right down for the next page.

questions.q: Where is Olive sitting at the start?
Where does Olive shelter from the wind?
How can you tell the wind is getting stronger as the story goes on?

preTeach.note: A gust is a sudden strong rush of wind.

prosody.quote: Olive is ready for a rainy day.
prosody.how: Read with quiet contentment on the last line.

questions.q: What does Olive pick from the bush?
What does a gust of wind do to Olive's pile?
Why does Olive set a flat stone on top the second time?
What does "gust" mean?
How do you know Olive's plan worked in the end?

cards.fluencyNote: New alternative pronunciations: ou as u, ear as er, or as er.

cards.title: Pip Waits Out the Storm in the Compost Heap
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 continues (School readiness) — new graphemes eigh, ei, ey.

preTeach.note: Blowing out air hard, like wind blowing strongly.

prosody.quote: Pip hops out, dry and warm.
prosody.how: Read with calm relief on the last line.

questions.q: Where does Pip shelter from the storm?
What does the wind do round the heap?
Why does Pip feel warm inside the heap?
What does "huffs and puffs" mean?
How does Pip know it is safe to come out?

cards.fluencyNote: New graphemes: eigh, ei, ey.

cards.title: Fig Pours Too Much
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 continues (School readiness) — new graphemes ore, oor, our.

preTeach.note: A gardener is a person whose job is looking after plants.

prosody.quote: The window box gets too wet.
prosody.how: Slow down slightly on "too wet" to show it is a problem.

questions.q: What was Fig watching the gardener do?
What happened to the shoots after Fig poured too much water?
Why do you think Fig felt bad about the mess?
What does it mean for a shoot to droop?
What did Fig learn by the end of the book?

cards.fluencyNote: New graphemes: ore, oor, our. Show contrast with voice between "Fig pours too much" (heavy, fast) and "Fig pours just a little bit" (light, careful).

cards.title: Nell and the Best Spot
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 continues (School readiness) — new graphemes ore, oor, our.

preTeach.note: Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another.

prosody.quote: Nell gets the best turn: the last one.
prosody.how: Read with a warm, satisfied tone — Nell is pleased, not disappointed, to go last.

questions.q: Who all wanted the bright spot on the path?
Why could not all four of them fit in the spot?
Who sat in the spot first?
What does it mean to take turns?
Why do you think Nell is happy to go last?

cards.fluencyNote: New graphemes: ore, oor, our. The three repeated lines "___ wants the spot too." are a good fluency builder — by the third one it should read smoothly.

cards.title: All About Earthworms
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 complete (School readiness) — non-fiction, Phonics Screening Check review week, real facts about earthworms.

preTeach.note: Soil is the earth that plants grow in.

prosody.quote: More worms come up when it rains.
prosody.how: Read at a steady, informative pace, like sharing a fact.

questions.q: Where does Moss find the worm?
What does a worm dig under the ground?
Why does a worm dig tunnels?
Why do worms help plants grow well?
When do more worms come up to the surface?

cards.fluencyNote: Phonics Screening Check review week, non-fiction. Several facts start with "A worm..." — read each as its own confident statement.

cards.title: Pip Cleans Up the Barn
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 complete (School readiness) — Phonics Screening Check review week, practising across the whole code.

preTeach.note: Straw is dry, golden stalks of plants, often used for animal bedding.

prosody.quote: Pip did not make this mess.
prosody.how: Read with a slightly defensive tone, as if Pip wants to make this clear.

questions.q: What did Pip find in the old barn?
What two things does Pip do to tidy up?
Why do you think Pip tidies up even though he did not make the mess?
What does neat and tidy mean?
Why do you think Moss looks surprised when he sees the barn?

cards.fluencyNote: Phonics Screening Check review week. The tidying actions each get their own page — read them as a clear sequence, one calm step at a time.

cards.title: Olive Tries a New Snack
cards.checkpoint: Year 1 Spring 2, week 4 — School readiness — Phase 5: new ways to say and spell ore, oor, our

preTeach.note: A compost heap is a pile where old plants and scraps break down into rich soil.

prosody.quote: Olive grins. The new snack is good after all.
prosody.how: Read "after all" with a warm, surprised smile — Olive did not expect to like it.

questions.q: Where did Olive find the new snack?
Who encouraged Olive to try one more bite?
Why do you think Olive pulled a face on the first bite?
What does it mean to pull a face?
Why do you think it is good to try new things, even if they seem strange at first?

cards.fluencyNote: Phonics Screening Check review week. Read "Olive pulls a face" with a scrunched-up, surprised voice, then "Olive grins" warmly at the end.

cards.title: Jumping and Splashing
cards.checkpoint: Year 1 Summer 2, week 2 — School readiness — Phase 6: new sounds -ing, -ed

preTeach.note: Squawked means made a loud, harsh bird-like shout.

prosody.quote: Pip was flapping and shouting and dripping all at the same time.
prosody.how: Read with breathless energy, almost tripping over the list of three -ing words.

questions.q: Who stayed up on the fence instead of getting wet?
What happened to Fig at the end?
Why do you think Pip "did too" at the end, after he would not jump in at the start?
What is Fig "best at", according to the story?

cards.fluencyNote: Listen for the three different sounds '-ed' makes in this book: jumped (/t/), rolled (/d/) and landed (/id/) — same spelling, different sound; no need to explain the rule, just notice it together.

cards.title: The Longest Day
cards.checkpoint: Year 1 Summer 2, week 4 — School readiness — Phase 6: new sounds -er, -est

preTeach.note: Shade is a cooler, shadowed spot out of direct sunlight.

prosody.quote: "The longest day," said Moss, "and I think this is the longest nap."
prosody.how: Read Moss's line slowly and sleepily, trailing off on 'nap' like he's about to doze off.

questions.q: Who did Ned say he was faster than?
What was Moss the softest and roundest of?
Why do you think the shade under the oak was "the best spot" as the day got hotter?
What does "the smallest" mean, compared to "small" and "smaller"?
What do "long", "longer" and "longest" all have in common?

cards.fluencyNote: Watch that the root word stays clearly recognisable before each ending — 'long' should still sound like 'long' inside 'longest', not get swallowed.

cards.title: Boxes and Bushes
cards.checkpoint: Year 1 Summer 2, week 4 — School readiness — Phase 6: new sounds -er, -est

preTeach.note: Hundreds means a very large number — many hundreds.

prosody.quote: "Next time," said Olive, "we get bigger boxes."
prosody.how: A wry, tired-but-amused tone — Olive has learned her lesson.

questions.q: What was Moss collecting the nuts for?
Why did they end up needing bigger boxes?
Why do you think Nell thought she had seen "five hundred" nuts when there were only five?
Why does "box" become "boxes" but most words just add "s"?

cards.fluencyNote: Check whether the extra syllable is added correctly on -es words (boxes, bushes, dishes) rather than reading them like a plain -s plural.

cards.title: Pip and the Little Frog
cards.listeningFocus: Oral storytelling and new vocabulary — putting your own words to what is happening in each picture, since there is no text to read.
joinIn: Page 2: point to the tangled frog and ask the child to describe how it looks.
Page 4: wiggle your fingers like pondweed being pulled loose, the way Pip tugs with his beak.
Page 6: both say how you think Pip and the frog are feeling now, in the sun.
talkPrompts: Pip is flying low over the pond — what do you think he has spotted down in the reeds?
Pip has landed right next to the frog — what do you think he is about to do?
Pip and the little frog are sitting together in the sun now — how do you think they both feel?

preTeach.note: A froglet is a very young, small frog.

cards.title: Ned and the Big Oak
cards.listeningFocus: Weather vocabulary and sequencing — noticing how the pictures show a change happening, start to finish.
joinIn: Page 2: look together at the leaves starting to swirl and name the weather word for it.
Page 4: waddle quickly on the spot the way Ned hurries to the tree.
Page 6: both say what the weather is doing by the last page, compared with the first.
talkPrompts: It is a calm, sunny day by the big oak tree — what do you think might change?
The sky is getting darker and the wind is stronger — how do you think Ned feels now?
The rain has stopped and the sun is coming out — how do you think Ned feels now?

preTeach.note: A shelter is a safe, dry place to wait out bad weather.

cards.title: Olive Builds a Nest
cards.listeningFocus: Sequencing and prediction — guessing what Olive needs next before turning the page.
joinIn: Page 2: both pretend to fly off and grab an imaginary twig, like Olive.
Page 4: name the soft materials Olive adds to her nest.
Page 6: both say how Olive looks, now the job is finished.
talkPrompts: Olive's nest looks a little bare and empty — what do you think she needs to do?
Olive is weaving the twig into her nest — what do you think the nest needs next?
Olive is curled up in her nest as it gets dark — how do you think she feels after all that work?

preTeach.note: To weave means to cross things over and under each other to join them together.

cards.title: Moss and the Wobbly Cane
cards.listeningFocus: Cause and effect — talking through why the first try does not work and what changes for the second.
joinIn: Page 2: lean sideways together, like the wobbly cane.
Page 4: cross your arms in an X shape, like Moss's two canes.
Page 6: both say why you think the second try worked better.
talkPrompts: This bean plant is leaning right over — what do you think could help it stand up?
The cane has slipped and fallen — how do you think Moss is feeling right now?
Moss looks proud of the vegetable patch now — why do you think plants sometimes need a little help like this?

preTeach.note: A cane is a thin stick used in gardens to help a plant stand up straight.

cards.title: Fig and the Round Thing
cards.listeningFocus: Curiosity and description — using your senses to guess what something might be.
joinIn: Page 3: roll a finger across the table, the way Fig nudges the round thing.
Page 4: both sniff the air, the way Fig sniffs the round thing.
Page 6: talk about where Fig decides to keep his treasure safe.
talkPrompts: Fig has spotted something round and shiny below — what do you think it could be?
Fig is trying to roll the round thing — what do you think will happen?
Fig still does not know what the round thing is, but how does he feel about it?

preTeach.note: A treasure is something kept carefully because it feels special, even if it is small.

cards.title: Nell's Race
cards.listeningFocus: Talking about feelings and kindness — what matters more than coming first.
joinIn: Page 2: race your fingers across the table, like Nell and Pip.
Page 4: gently nudge an imaginary beetle to safety with one finger.
Page 6: both decide how you think Nell feels at the very end.
talkPrompts: Nell and Pip are lined up ready to race across the stream — who do you think will win?
Pip has reached the other side first, but Nell has stopped — what has she noticed?
Pip does not seem to mind that Nell was last — why do you think that is?

preTeach.note: Glum means feeling a bit sad or disappointed.

cards.title: Pip's Rainy Day Box
cards.listeningFocus: Imagination and making things — talking about what Pip makes from found objects.
joinIn: Page 2: pretend to pick up a tiny piece of string, like Pip.
Page 5: both guess what Pip is building before you see the result.
Page 6: name each of the three things Pip used in his little sailboat.
talkPrompts: It is raining outside the barn — what do you think Pip could do on a day like this?
Pip is arranging his found treasures — what do you think he is making?
Pip looks very pleased with his rainy-day project — how do you think he feels?

preTeach.note: Straw is the dry, golden stalks left over from a crop like wheat.

cards.title: Ned Calls Out
cards.listeningFocus: A true animal fact — noticing how calling out loudly helps Ned be found.
joinIn: Page 3: open your mouth wide and call out, like Ned.
Page 4: both cup a hand behind an ear, like Olive listening hard.
Page 6: say how you think Ned feels now his friends are back.
talkPrompts: Ned is following behind Moss and Olive through the tall grass — can you see he is falling a little behind?
Ned has opened his beak wide — what do you think he is doing?
Ned has been found — how do you think he feels now that his friends are back?

preTeach.note: To be reunited means to be brought back together after being apart.

cards.title: Olive's Big Job
cards.listeningFocus: Teamwork and asking for help — noticing the difference between page 1 and page 4.
joinIn: Page 1: push against an imaginary log by yourself, like Olive.
Page 3: wave an arm to call for help, like Olive calling Moss.
Page 6: both say what you think they found under the log.
talkPrompts: Olive is trying to push a big log by herself — is it working?
Now there are two of them pushing — do you think that will make a difference?
Look what was hiding under the log — how do you think Olive and Moss feel about doing the job together?

preTeach.note: A hollow is a small empty, scooped-out space.

cards.title: Moss Tidies the Bird Table
cards.listeningFocus: Kindness and tidying up — talking about doing something helpful without being asked.
joinIn: Page 3: pretend to gather up scattered seeds into a little pile.
Page 4: sweep an arm like a little broom, the way Moss uses his twig.
Page 6: say who comes to visit the tidy bird table at the end.
talkPrompts: The bird table looks very messy — what do you think happened here?
Moss is gathering up the scattered seeds — where do you think he is putting them?
A new visitor has come to the tidy bird table — how do you think Moss feels watching?

preTeach.note: Scattered means spread out messily in lots of different places.

cards.title: A Sunny Day
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 (School readiness) — new sound 'ay' (the /ai/ sound at the end of a word)

preTeach.note: Dried grass, often used for animals to lie on or eat.

prosody.quote: Splash! May Pip get wet?
prosody.how: Punchy "Splash!", then read the question with real rising question-intonation on "wet".

questions.q: What was the weather like in this story?
Where did Ned run to first?
Why do you think Pip didn't want to stay in the sun?
What does "soft hay" feel like, do you think?
What time of year do you think this story is set in? Why?

cards.fluencyNote: First Phase 5 book — the new spelling 'ay' should read exactly like the 'ai' already known from 'rain'; hesitation only on ay-words is the one new thing to practise.

cards.title: Five White Kites
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 (School readiness) — new sound 'i-e' (the split spelling as in kite, five and white)

preTeach.note: Here "cross" means grumpy or a little angry, not an X shape.

prosody.quote: "Nine trees," she said. "It went nine trees."
prosody.how: Read Olive's line a little breathlessly and proudly, like she's just got her breath back from chasing it.

questions.q: How many kites did Pip have?
What happened to the string on one kite?
Why was Fig unsure about the kites at first?
What does it mean if Olive is "quick when she is cross"?
Why do you think Fig held his string "as tight as tight" at the end?

cards.fluencyNote: 'i-e' is a THIRD spelling of this sound (after igh and ie) — 'kite' should now be read effortlessly as one blended word, not sounded out letter by letter.

cards.title: The Blue Phone
cards.checkpoint: Phase 5 complete (School readiness) — a mixed book for 'ue', 'ph' and 'wh' (blue, phone, when)

preTeach.note: A grin is a big, wide smile.

prosody.quote: "When did that get there?" said Pip. "And what is it for?"
prosody.how: Two real questions — let the pitch rise clearly at the end of each one.

questions.q: What colour was the phone Nell found?
Who turns out to own the phone?
Why do you think Olive believed the phone "keeps what it sees"?
Which two letters make the /f/ sound in "phone"?
Why did they decide to leave the phone in the grass at the end?

cards.fluencyNote: Three tricky spellings land together here (ue, ph, wh) — a smooth read of 'phone' without stumbling on 'ph' is a strong sign the whole Phase 5 code is becoming automatic.

cards.title: Ned Is Unsure
cards.checkpoint: Phase 6 (School readiness) — the prefixes 'un-' and 'dis-' (sure → unsure, appear → disappear)

preTeach.note: A reed is a tall, thin plant that grows near water.

prosody.quote: "I disagree," said Nell. "I do not think it went. I think it is under a reed."
prosody.how: Read Nell's line firmly and a little stubbornly — she's contradicting Olive.

questions.q: What had gone missing at the start of the story?
Where did they find it in the end?
What does the word "unsure" tell you about how Ned was feeling?
If "appear" means to show up, what does "disappear" mean?
How did adding 'un-' and 'dis-' change the meaning of the root words in this story?

cards.fluencyNote: Nell has two short disagreements before the reed is found — read each "I do not think" a little more insistently than the last, building towards the reveal.
